boundary: Reference navigation only. A pathway links public reference sections and the registered sources and release findings behind them. A pathway step is not an Atlas relationship and asserts no industrial dependency; the Dependency Evidence Atlas is the only place a dependency is approved. No pathway carries a score, a ranking, a readiness verdict or an approval.

evidence_classes.verified_fact: Stated by the body that defines it, or independently established
evidence_classes.attributed_statement: What a company, consortium or agency published, not independently verified
evidence_classes.bounded_analysis: The project's arithmetic or classification, with stated assumptions
evidence_classes.not_supported: A claim the reviewed evidence does not support

comparison_verdicts.valid: Same quantity, unit, direction, scope and basis
comparison_verdicts.conditional: Comparable only with a stated condition or an unresolved conflict recorded
comparison_verdicts.unsupported: Different quantities, scopes or generations; no comparison should be drawn

pathways.title: HBM to advanced packaging
pathways.research_question: How do high-bandwidth memory architecture and advanced packaging interact in AI accelerator integration, and which industrial dependencies are actually documented?
pathways.technical_purpose: Take a researcher from the HBM4 interface specification to the specific packaging evidence an integration claim would need, separating technology architecture from product-level qualification.

scope.technical: HBM4 and HBM4E stacks and interposer-class packaging as disclosed by JEDEC, memory suppliers, TSMC and AMD

assumptions: Supplier and foundry statements describe their own products and plans, not third-party integration
The MI300X case is used because it is the only accelerator in the reviewed evidence with a disclosed package technology
limitations: MI300X uses HBM3, not HBM4; no reviewed source names the package technology of a specific HBM4 accelerator
The JEDEC and UCIe normative texts were not reviewed; only announcements were
No qualification record linking a named HBM4 stack to a named accelerator package was reviewed

steps.title: Start from the HBM4 interface definition
steps.relevance: The 2,048-bit interface and 32 channels per stack fix how many signal paths each stack presents to the package, which is the first physical constraint on integration.

scope.technical: Per stack, as announced for JESD270-4

limitations: An announcement, not the normative standard
Defines the interface, not any product's speed grade
steps.next_evidence: The normative JESD270-4 text, including timing and any speed bins above 8 Gb/s

steps.title: Check stated speeds against the interface arithmetic
steps.relevance: Supplier pin rates above JEDEC's announced 8 Gb/s mean that conforming to the interface does not fix the speed a package must carry; the speed grade is a product-level property.

scope.technical: Per-stack peak bandwidth from width × pin rate

limitations: Peak arithmetic, not sustained or application bandwidth
Speed grades above 8 Gb/s are supplier statements
steps.next_evidence: Qualified speed grades for named stacks on named accelerator platforms

steps.title: Trace the base logic die to its fabrication route
steps.relevance: An HBM4 stack sits on a logic base die, so memory integration also depends on a logic fabrication process that differs by supplier.

scope.technical: Base-die sourcing as each supplier states it

limitations: Process nodes are unstated for SK hynix and Micron HBM4 base dies
That HBM4 adds an external dependency for SK hynix is the release's inference
steps.next_evidence: Process-node disclosures for each supplier's HBM4 base die

steps.title: Follow the stack into the package
steps.relevance: Stacking methods (MR-MUF, hybrid bonding) and foundry packaging plans are where memory meets packaging; they are disclosed as capabilities, not as the package of any named HBM4 accelerator.

scope.technical: Stack assembly and HBM-to-CoWoS statements

limitations: Hybrid bonding is not stated as used in HBM4 or HBM4E
TSMC's 9.5-reticle CoWoS for 12 or more stacks is a 2027 plan
The 2024 SK hynix and TSMC memorandum states an aim, not a shipped integration
steps.next_evidence: Per-product interposer, substrate, assembly-site and stack-test disclosures

steps.title: Compare the interposer and bridge platforms
steps.relevance: Interposer size bounds how many HBM stacks fit beside the logic dies; TSMC reports every size above 3.3 reticles as CoWoS-L.

scope.technical: TSMC CoWoS variants and interposer sizes

limitations: TSMC's 2025 report states the 5.5-reticle CoWoS-L status two different ways
Capacity and customer allocation are not disclosed
steps.next_evidence: TSMC confirmation of 5.5-reticle CoWoS-L qualification and volume status

steps.title: Read one product-level disclosure, and its generation
steps.relevance: MI300X is the reviewed product whose maker names its package technology and memory connections, which shows the kind of disclosure an HBM4 integration claim would need. It uses HBM3, so it is not HBM4 evidence.

scope.technical: AMD Instinct MI300X as AMD describes it

limitations: The CoWoS variant and interposer size of MI300X are not stated
HBM3 generation; does not transfer to HBM4 products
steps.next_evidence: An equivalent disclosure for a named HBM4 accelerator

steps.title: Separate interface standards from integration and interoperability
steps.relevance: Interface standards (JEDEC HBM4, UCIe) define how dies talk; they do not establish that a given stack and package work together, which needs product-level test results.

scope.technical: UCIe scope and the distinction between standard, integration and interoperability

limitations: No published cross-vendor interoperability result was reviewed
steps.next_evidence: Published compliance or interoperability results for named products

steps.title: Record what is not established: qualification and substitution
steps.relevance: Supplier statements that a stack is designed for a platform are the closest evidence to qualification, and they stop short of it.

scope.technical: Supplier design-target statements for NVIDIA Vera Rubin

limitations: Does not establish NVIDIA qualification, interchangeable supply or multi-sourcing
steps.next_evidence: Accelerator-maker qualification disclosures naming memory suppliers and speed grades

statements.text: JEDEC's HBM4 announcement defines a 2,048-bit interface with 32 channels per stack.
Every HBM4 stack depends on two manufacturing capabilities, a DRAM process and a logic base-die process, before any packaging.
Interface conformance and package integration are separate claims; neither establishes that a named stack is qualified in a named package.
No reviewed source names the interposer, substrate or assembly provider for any named HBM4 accelerator.
MI300X packaging evidence cannot be carried over to HBM4 products, because MI300X uses HBM3.

next_evidence: Per-product package disclosures for a named HBM4 accelerator: interposer or bridge, substrate, assembly site
Accelerator-maker qualification records naming HBM4 suppliers and speed grades
The normative JESD270-4 and UCIe specification texts

pathways.title: Memory bandwidth to system data movement
pathways.research_question: How do memory bandwidth, accelerator interconnects, and scale-out networking differ, and why are their published performance figures not automatically comparable?
pathways.technical_purpose: Show which bandwidth comparisons are technically valid, which hold only under stated conditions, and which are unsupported, by keeping each figure's unit, direction, scope and basis attached to it.

scope.technical: Peak bandwidth figures for HBM stacks, accelerator memory, on-package fabric, scale-up, host links and scale-out

assumptions: All figures are vendor-stated peaks or arithmetic from them
A comparison is valid only when unit, direction, scope and basis match
limitations: No measured, effective or workload-level bandwidth was reviewed for any system
MI300X (HBM3) and Rubin (HBM4) are different generations; GB200 NVL72 figures are rack-level

steps.title: Per-stack memory bandwidth
steps.relevance: Per-stack peak bandwidth is width × pin rate ÷ 8; it is the smallest memory quantity and the base of every per-device figure.

scope.technical: Per stack, peak

limitations: Peak, not sustained
A combined read and write capability, not a sum of two directions

steps.title: Per-accelerator memory bandwidth
steps.relevance: Device memory bandwidth sums all stacks on one package; NVIDIA gives two different figures for Rubin.

scope.technical: Per Rubin GPU, peak

limitations: 22 TB/s and 19.2 TB/s are both NVIDIA statements; the conflict is unresolved
steps.next_evidence: An NVIDIA specification stating which figure applies and on what basis

steps.title: On-package movement inside one accelerator
steps.relevance: Cache, die-to-die and memory paths inside a package carry their own figures, which are larger than and distinct from off-package links.

scope.technical: AMD MI300 Series on-package tiers

limitations: Two AMD L2 figures (34.4 TB/s and 51.6 TB/s) are not reconciled
steps.next_evidence: AMD clarification of its L2 bandwidth figures

steps.title: Where memory bandwidth ends and fabric bandwidth begins
steps.relevance: Memory and fabric figures measure different physical paths; their ratio is a magnitude, not a statement of how fast a GPU reaches a peer.

scope.technical: Ratios of stated peaks across measurement domains

limitations: Ratios depend on whether AMD's bidirectional 896 GB/s figure is per GPU, which AMD does not state
steps.next_evidence: AMD confirmation of whether 896 GB/s is a per-GPU, both-direction sum

steps.title: Accelerator-to-accelerator scale-up fabrics
steps.relevance: Scale-up figures are stated per GPU, per link or per rack, in bytes, sometimes bidirectional and sometimes with no direction stated.

scope.technical: MI300X 8-GPU platform, Vera Rubin NVL72 and GB200 NVL72 scale-up figures

limitations: AMD states that 896 GB/s is bidirectional but not whether it is per GPU or per platform
NVIDIA gives 3.6 TB/s and 3.0 TB/s for NVLink 6 per Rubin GPU, and its current product pages split the same way
steps.next_evidence: Per-link bandwidth, direction and encoding disclosures from AMD and NVIDIA

steps.title: Host and CPU connections
steps.relevance: Host links (PCIe, CXL, NVLink-C2C) use per-link figures whose raw totals count both directions unless stated otherwise.

scope.technical: x16 host links and coherent CPU-GPU links

limitations: Raw rates exclude encoding and protocol overhead
Whether MI300X or Rubin implement CXL is not established
steps.next_evidence: PCI-SIG specification statements on payload efficiency

steps.title: Leaving the scale-up domain
steps.relevance: Scale-out networking changes the dependency model as well as the bandwidth: NICs and switches replace the scale-up fabric.

scope.technical: Vera Rubin NVL72 scale-out and the Ultra Ethernet network types

limitations: The 1.6 Tb/s per-GPU figure has no stated direction
steps.next_evidence: Direction and measurement basis of per-GPU scale-out figures

steps.title: Apply the six checks before any comparison
steps.relevance: Bits or bytes, transfers or payload, direction, scope, peak or sustained, and who measured it decide whether two figures can be compared.

scope.technical: Unit and direction alignment for stated figures

limitations: No measured figure was reviewed
steps.next_evidence: Published collective or application bandwidth with a stated workload and method

comparisons.reason: Both are per-stack peak bandwidths for a 2,048-bit HBM4 interface, differing only in pin rate.

Both are NVIDIA per-GPU memory figures for Rubin, but they conflict, and NVIDIA's current product pages split the same way (22 TB/s on HGX, 19.2 TB/s on Vera Rubin NVL72); either can be used only with its date and source until NVIDIA explains the difference.
Both are per-accelerator peak memory bandwidth, but across HBM3 and HBM4 generations; they compare stated peaks, not delivered throughput.

AMD states that 896 GB/s is bidirectional but not whether it is per GPU or per platform, and NVIDIA publishes NVLink 6 per Rubin GPU as both 3.6 TB/s and 3 TB/s; across two vendors and two generations, the pair shows neither relative fabric capability nor achieved bandwidth.
Memory and NVLink figures describe different physical paths; their ratio does not show how fast a GPU reaches local versus peer memory.
One is a GB200 NVL72 rack aggregate and the other a per-GPU Rubin figure that NVIDIA also publishes as 3 TB/s: different scopes and different generations.

Not comparable as one metric: 3.6 TB/s is NVLink 6 per-GPU fabric bandwidth to the NVLink Switch, stated bidirectional, and 1.6 Tb/s is ConnectX-9 per-GPU network-port bandwidth with no stated direction, on a different path, interface and counting basis. Converting bits to bytes puts both in one unit but does not make them the same quantity. As arithmetic on advertised figures only, the first is about 9x or 18x the second depending on that direction; the ratio says nothing about delivered throughput. NVIDIA also publishes NVLink 6 as 3 TB/s per GPU.
Both describe x16 links at the PCIe 6.0 rate, but NVIDIA does not state that its figure uses the same both-direction raw basis.

statements.text: Per-stack HBM4 bandwidth follows from interface width and pin rate, and every disclosed figure is consistent with a 2,048-bit interface.
NVIDIA states 22 TB/s and, later, 19.2 TB/s for Rubin memory bandwidth.
Whether AMD's 896 GB/s figure is per GPU or per platform remains unresolved; AMD states that it is bidirectional.
No reviewed source reports measured collective or application bandwidth, so no workload-level comparison is supported.

next_evidence: Measured collective bandwidth with a stated workload, configuration and method
AMD per-link bandwidth and direction for MI300X Infinity Fabric
NVIDIA resolution of the Rubin memory and NVLink 6 figure conflicts

pathways.title: AI accelerator rack to deployable compute
pathways.research_question: What separates a documented AI accelerator rack architecture from evidence of installed, commissioned, and operational computing infrastructure?
pathways.technical_purpose: Follow one documented rack, GB200 NVL72, through hardware, fabric, power, cooling, software, operations and access, and show what evidence would support each stronger operational statement.

scope.technical: NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 racks and the DGX SuperPOD reference architecture
scope.temporal: Sources dated 2024-10-15 to 2026-11-09; releases compiled 2026-11-09 to 2026-11-10

assumptions: GB200 only; where NVIDIA covers GB200 and GB300 together that is recorded
Vera Rubin figures are not used in this pathway
limitations: Every reviewed source is a product description, reference architecture or procedure; none is a site record
Power, cooling, firmware and acceptance criteria are partly undefined in the reviewed sources

steps.title: The documented rack
steps.relevance: The rack's composition (18 compute trays, 9 NVLink switch trays, power shelves, bus bar, manifolds) is the product specification every later requirement refers to.

scope.technical: DGX GB rack systems as NVIDIA describes them

limitations: The user guide covers GB200 and GB300 together
steps.next_evidence: Separate GB200 and GB300 specifications

steps.title: The rack's scale-up fabric
steps.relevance: The NVLink domain spans the rack, so its configuration is a rack-level requirement, stated by NVIDIA as a rack aggregate.

scope.technical: GB200 NVL72 aggregate NVLink bandwidth

limitations: A rack aggregate, not a per-GPU or measured figure

steps.title: Electrical delivery to the rack
steps.relevance: Power shelves and a DC bus bar define what the facility must feed; NVIDIA's documents disagree on redundancy and leave the rack figure's basis undefined.

scope.technical: Rack power distribution as NVIDIA describes it

limitations: N+N in the user guide, N in the reference architecture
1,400 A at about 50 V is about 70 kW against about 120 kW
steps.next_evidence: An NVIDIA power specification stating redundancy, bus-bar paths and figure basis

steps.title: From rack to scalable unit
steps.relevance: Facility planning uses the 1.2 MW scalable-unit design figure, which exceeds eight racks at about 120 kW by an unitemised 0.24 MW.

scope.technical: Eight-rack scalable unit

limitations: A design value, not measured consumption
steps.next_evidence: An NVIDIA breakdown of the scalable-unit figure

steps.title: Heat removal and the facility loop
steps.relevance: Liquid cooling through cold plates hands heat to a facility loop via a CDU; the coolant parameters a site must supply are not stated.

scope.technical: Hybrid liquid and air cooling; CDU terminology

limitations: No coolant type, flow, supply temperature, pressure or class is stated
The liquid and air shares are not stated
steps.next_evidence: NVIDIA site-preparation or facility-interface specifications

steps.title: Software, firmware and orchestration
steps.relevance: The stack spans compute, switch and power-shelf firmware, with orchestration support stated differently by guide version.

scope.technical: Mission Control and DGX software as documented

limitations: The 2025 guide describes Slurm only; the 2.5.0 rack-setup guide adds Kubernetes through RunAI
Required firmware and software versions are not in the reviewed documents
steps.next_evidence: The DGX GB200/GB300 Firmware Update Guide and Mission Control release notes

steps.title: Operations: network, leak response, tested scale
steps.relevance: Operating the rack couples cluster software to building management and the facility network; NVIDIA's tested scale is stated two ways.

scope.technical: Operations as documented by NVIDIA

limitations: The building-management interface is not specified
Two SUs or one: the reference architecture says both
steps.next_evidence: An NVIDIA building-management interface specification; a corrected reference architecture

steps.title: Access and compliance
steps.relevance: Export controls attach to items, destinations, end uses and parties, so they govern who may receive and use the rack.

scope.technical: US export controls as announced on 2024-12-02

limitations: Beyond the 2024 announcement, only two current sections, 15 CFR 742.6 and 740.25, were reviewed (2026-11-11); other applicable provisions were not
Not legal advice
steps.next_evidence: The other provisions that apply to a named item, such as its ECCN entry, and a determination for a named transaction

steps.title: From documented to operational: the evidence states
steps.relevance: Each stronger operational statement needs a different kind of record; vendor documents reach only the first two states.

scope.technical: Evidence states for GB200 NVL72 requirements

limitations: No site record was reviewed
NVIDIA's checklist states no acceptance thresholds
steps.next_evidence: Installation, commissioning and operating records for a named site

evidence_ladder.supported_statement: NVIDIA documents the rack's configuration and requirements.
evidence_ladder.record_required: A vendor product description or specification

evidence_ladder.supported_statement: A reference architecture proposes how racks are combined and supplied.
evidence_ladder.record_required: A reference architecture or a site design

evidence_ladder.supported_statement: A named site has contracted the capacity or service.
evidence_ladder.record_required: A contract or service agreement for a named site

evidence_ladder.supported_statement: Racks were delivered to a named site.
Racks are installed at a named site; this does not establish commissioning.
A subsystem passed its commissioning tests.
evidence_ladder.record_required: A commissioning test result for one subsystem

evidence_ladder.supported_statement: Subsystems were tested together under stated conditions.
Measured operation over a stated period.
evidence_ladder.record_required: Measurements from operation over a stated period

evidence_ladder.supported_statement: No record of the kind needed was found; the requirement is unshown, not unmet.

statements.text: NVIDIA documents the GB200 NVL72 rack configuration, power distribution and cooling architecture.
Vendor documents reach the product-specification and proposed-infrastructure states only; later states need site records.
Redundancy, bus-bar paths, the basis of 120 kW, coolant parameters and acceptance criteria remain undefined.
A reference architecture or a vendor checklist does not establish that any rack is installed, commissioned or operating.

next_evidence: Installation, commissioning and operating records for a named site
NVIDIA power, coolant and acceptance specifications for GB200 NVL72
The GB200/GB300 firmware update guide and version-specific software support
